line: e4 c5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Ne5
teaches: When an enemy bishop is planted on a square your knight can hit, jumping in to attack it can win the bishop pair even without a fork — forcing the trade and driving the piece behind it to an awkward square is a real gain in the opening.
explains: The knight leaps to e5, hitting the bishop on c4 and the queen on f3 at the same time. White cannot save the bishop, so Black walks away with the pair of bishops and shoves the queen onto a more exposed square. No fork needed — the double attack does the work.

line: e4 c5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Ne5 Qb3 Nxc4 Qxc4
teaches: Trading a knight for a bishop is a clear gain when you come out with the two bishops and provoke the enemy queen onto an exposed square — a queen stuck in the open becomes a target your development can hit with tempo.
explains: After the swap Black holds the bishop pair, and look where the white queen sits — out in the open on c4. That is not a loss of the knight, it is a gain: Black's coming central expansion will hit the queen and gain time doing it.

line: e4 c5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Ne5 Qb3 Nxc4 Qxc4 e6
teaches: When you expand in the centre, choose the pawn move that prepares a break and keeps your pieces free over the passive one that blocks them in — flexibility is worth more than a solid but stodgy structure.
explains: You could shut things in with d6 — but e6 is more flexible. It prepares the d5 break and leaves the light-squared bishop free to choose its diagonal later. Black expands while keeping every option open, rather than boxing his own pieces in.
